title: Production
summary: ## Production function

Production is the transformation of inputs into output. Inputs are the resources used in production: land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship and raw materials. Output is the goods and services produced. To grow rice, for example, you need land, seeds, fertiliser, water, a plough and diesel.

The production function is the technical relationship between inputs and output. It shows the maximum output that can be produced from given quantities of inputs. There is a direct relationship between the amount of inputs and the amount of output. The ratio in which inputs are combined is called the technology (method) of production.
## Technologies of production

Labour-intensive technology uses more labour and less capital per unit of output, for example a handloom, or a wooden plough with bullocks. It is used in household enterprises, in small-scale production and in production for self-consumption.

Capital-intensive technology uses more capital and less labour per unit of output, for example a powerloom, or a tractor, pump set and harvester. It is used in large-scale production for sale, by corporations and government enterprises.
## Division of labour

Division of labour means splitting production into processes and giving each process to the worker best suited to it. It raises efficiency, makes large-scale production possible, leads to inventions, and encourages the use of machines and capital-intensive methods.

Product-based division of labour: a worker specialises in making a whole good or service. Examples are a potter, cobbler or carpenter in a village, and small farmers. It is common in household enterprises and small-scale production.

Process-based division of labour: production is split into many processes and each worker does one or two of them. Examples are a bread factory, where workers make dough, bake, cut and pack, and street lighting, where different teams fix poles, wiring, bulbs and supply. It is used in large units.
## TP, AP and MP
Total product (TP) is the total output at a given level of a variable input such as labour, with all other inputs fixed.
Average product (AP) is output per unit of labour: AP = TP ÷ L. For example, 5 workers with TP 95 give AP = 95 ÷ 5 = 19.

Marginal product (MP) is the change in TP from one more unit of labour: MP = TP(L) − TP(L−1). It is the output added by the last worker. If 1 worker stitches 2 shirts and 2 workers stitch 6, MP of the second worker = 6 − 2 = 4.
## Law of diminishing marginal product

When more and more labour is added to a fixed factor such as a machine, MP first rises, then falls, and can become negative. When MP is zero, TP is at its maximum. A producer should stop adding labour before MP becomes negative.
## Production process, firm and industry

The production process involves arranging the factors from their owners, combining them in the right proportion, buying and storing raw materials, producing, storing and selling the output. The entrepreneur organises it.
A firm is a single production unit, such as Bata. An industry is the group of all firms making the same commodity, such as the shoe industry.

Firms and industries are important because they (1) provide goods and services for consumption, (2) provide goods for investment such as machines and vehicles, (3) give employment, and (4) provide infrastructure — energy, transport, communication, health, education and housing.
## Types of producers

Indigenous units are located in the country and owned by its residents. Examples are farms, shops, factories, schools, and self-employed doctors, lawyers and teachers. They may be private or government units.
Private units are of five kinds:
(a) Sole proprietorship has one owner.
(b) Partnership has 2 to 20 owners (the maximum is 20).
(c) Company: a private company has 2 to 50 shareholders; a public company has at least 7 and no maximum. Companies are formed under the Companies Act 1956.
(d) Cooperative society is a voluntary association for mutual benefit with at least 10 members and no maximum, formed under the Cooperative Societies Act 1912. Kendriya Bhandar is an example.
(e) Private non-profit organisations include charitable hospitals and schools.

Government units are of two kinds. Departmental enterprises are directly controlled by a ministry, such as Indian Railways, All India Radio and Doordarshan. Public sector undertakings are autonomous corporations, such as HMT, MMTC, LIC, GIC, IOC and Indian Airlines.

Foreign units are located in the country but owned by non-residents, who contribute more than 50% of the capital. Multinationals have their head office in one country and work in many, e.g. Coca-Cola, Nokia, Samsung and Hyundai. Collaborations are jointly owned by Indian and foreign partners, e.g. Maruti-Suzuki.

vsa: What does a production function tell us?
It shows the technical relationship between inputs and output: the maximum output that can be produced from given quantities of inputs such as land, labour, capital and raw materials.

or: Land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship, combined with raw materials.

vsa: Distinguish between land and labour as factors of production.

Land is a free gift of nature — plains, mountains, plateaus, minerals and forests. It is limited and immobile.
Labour is human effort, physical or mental, used in production. It is supplied by people and earns wages.

Division of labour means splitting the production of a good into many processes and giving each process to the worker best suited to it. It raises efficiency and makes large-scale production possible.

or: Working capital is the raw material used up in a single round of production, such as yarn, clay, seeds and fertilisers. Fixed capital, by contrast, lasts many years.

vsa: Capital-intensive technology uses more capital and less labour per unit of output, e.g. a powerloom, or a tractor and harvester. It is used in large-scale production by corporations and government enterprises.
Explain the importance of firms and industries as a source of employment.
Most people get jobs in firms and industries and earn the income they need to satisfy their wants. Industries such as agriculture, textiles, transport and IT employ millions of people.

or: The production process involves getting factors from their owners, combining them in the right proportion, buying and storing raw materials, producing, storing and selling the output. The entrepreneur organises it.

vsa: What is meant by entrepreneurship as a factor of production?
Entrepreneurship is the art of organising production. The entrepreneur brings land, labour and capital together, takes decisions, bears risk and earns profit.
What is the importance of creating infrastructure?

Infrastructure means energy, transport, communication, health, education and housing. It is the base on which all production rests. Without it the all-round development of the country is not possible.
sa: Distinguish between labour-intensive and capital-intensive technology with examples.

Labour-intensive technology uses more labour and less capital per unit of output. Examples are a handloom, or a wooden plough with bullocks. It is used in small-scale, household and self-consumption production.
Capital-intensive technology uses more capital and less labour per unit of output. Examples are a powerloom, or a tractor, pump set and harvester. It is used in large-scale production for sale by corporations and government enterprises.
Distinguish between product-based and process-based division of labour with examples.

Product-based: a worker makes a whole good or service himself. Examples are a village potter, cobbler or carpenter, or a small farmer. It is common in small-scale production.
Process-based: production is split into many processes and each worker does one or two of them. In a bread factory, for example, different workers make dough, bake, cut and pack. It is used in large units, where nobody can claim to have made the whole product.
What is entrepreneurship? State the qualities of an entrepreneur.

Entrepreneurship is the art of organising production. The entrepreneur brings land, labour and capital together in the right proportion, takes decisions, bears risk and uncertainty, pays the other factors and earns profit.
Qualities: knowledge, courage to take risks, leadership, decision-making ability and organising ability.
Explain capital as a factor of production.

Capital is man-made wealth used in production: machines, tools, buildings and materials.
It raises the efficiency of land and labour, for example through irrigation and machines.
It is a passive factor that needs labour to work it, and it has a limited life and becomes obsolete.
Fixed capital lasts many years; working capital, such as raw materials, is used up.
Distinguish between fixed capital and working capital. Why is human resource important in production?

Fixed capital (machines, tractors, buildings) is used for many years. Working capital (yarn, seeds, fertiliser) is used up in one round of production.
Human resource: labour, physical and mental, skilled and unskilled, works the machines and land. Without it, capital, a passive factor, cannot be used. Education and training raise its productivity.
Explain the classification of foreign production units.

A foreign production unit is located in the country but more than 50% of its capital comes from non-residents.
(1) Multinationals have their head office in one country and business in many countries, e.g. Coca-Cola, Nokia, Samsung, Hyundai.
(2) Collaborations are owned jointly by Indian and foreign entrepreneurs, e.g. Maruti-Suzuki. They count as foreign if foreigners hold more than 50% of the capital.

or: A cooperative society is a voluntary association of persons for mutual benefit, working through self-help and collective effort. It is formed under the Cooperative Societies Act 1912, has at least 10 members and no upper limit, and divides profit according to shares. Examples are cooperative stores, housing societies and Kendriya Bhandar.

sa: Calculate AP and MP from the table: Labour 1, 2, 3, 4 — TP 10, 18, 24, 28.

AP = TP ÷ L: 10 ÷ 1 = 10; 18 ÷ 2 = 9; 24 ÷ 3 = 8; 28 ÷ 4 = 7.
MP = TP(L) − TP(L−1): 10 − 0 = 10; 18 − 10 = 8; 24 − 18 = 6; 28 − 24 = 4.
MP falls as labour increases — the law of diminishing marginal product.
la: Explain the role and importance of firms and industries.

A firm is a single production unit; an industry is all the firms making one commodity.
(1) Goods and services for consumption: they supply food, clothes, TV sets and services to satisfy growing wants.
(2) Goods for investment: they make machines, plants, buses, trucks, railways and ships.
(3) Employment: most people earn their income working in firms and industries.
(4) Infrastructure: they provide energy, transport, communication, health, education and housing, without which all-round development is not possible.
What is the production function? Explain TP, AP and MP with an example.

The production function is the technical relationship between inputs and output: the maximum output producible from given inputs.
TP is the total output at a given level of labour, with other inputs fixed.
AP = TP ÷ L, output per worker.
MP = TP(L) − TP(L−1), the output added by the last worker.
Example: with 3 workers TP = 36, so AP = 12. With 4 workers TP = 44, so MP of the 4th worker = 44 − 36 = 8 and AP = 11.
State and explain the law of diminishing marginal product of labour.

Law: when more units of a variable factor (labour) are added to fixed factors, MP first rises, then falls, and may become negative.
Reason: at first the extra workers share work efficiently, so MP rises. Beyond a point the fixed machine is over-used and extra workers add less and less.
Example: MP 10, 12, 14, then 8, 6, 4, 2, 0, −2. TP is at its maximum (56) when MP = 0, so labour should not be increased beyond that point.
Describe the types of private indigenous production units.

(1) Sole proprietorship: one owner, who bears all profit and loss and manages the unit.
(2) Partnership: 2 to 20 owners who manage jointly and share profit as agreed.
(3) Company: owned by shareholders; a private company has 2–50, a public company at least 7 and no maximum (Companies Act 1956). Directors manage it.
(4) Cooperative society: at least 10 members, voluntary, for mutual benefit (Act 1912), e.g. Kendriya Bhandar.
(5) Private non-profit organisations: charitable schools and hospitals that serve society, not profit.
